prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BERLIN, Germany (CNN) -- A German cruise liner said Tuesday it plans to fly its passengers over the Gulf of Aden, instead of sailing them through, out of fear of pirate attacks in the region. U.S. Navy image of pirates operating off coast of Somalia in October this year. Hapag-Lloyd Cruises said all 246 passengers and most of the crew aboard the MS Columbus, currently at the start of an around-the-world cruise, will disembark at an undisclosed port, then fly to Dubai to continue their journey. The company called the move a precautionary measure. Pirate attacks in the waters off Somalia have shot up this year, with pirates staging increasingly bolder attacks on ever-bigger targets. So far this year, pirates have attacked almost 100 vessels off Somalia's coast and successfully hijacked nearly 40, according to the International Maritime Bureau. Freight and cargo ships, cruise liners, and private yachts have all come under attack. In many hijackings, pirates take the crew and passengers hostage while they demand a ransom. The problem has forced companies like Hapag-Lloyd, that use the Gulf of Aden, to make new plans, including stepping up security or changing their routes. One shipping company announced last month it would bypass the region altogether, sailing instead around the Cape of Good Hope and adding thousands of kilometers to its voyages. Read more about how to solve the pirate problem here. Hapag-Lloyd said a general travel warning for the area, issued by the German Foreign Ministry, played a part in the decision. But the company also said it had asked the German government for naval protection and the request was turned down. Representatives of Hapag-Lloyd and the German Defense Ministry could not immediately be reached for further comment. The passengers on board the Columbus began the first leg of their world cruise November 28 in Genoa, Italy and are due in Dubai on December 17, according to Hapag-Lloyd's Web site. Further stops include Singapore, Bali, Indonesia and Sydney, Australia. Hapag-Lloyd said that after the passengers and most of the crew disembark, the Columbus will sail through the Gulf of Aden with a skeleton staff. The passengers will stay in a five-star hotel in Dubai for three days until the Columbus arrives to take them back onboard, the company said. Both the crew and passengers approve of the safety measure, Hapag-Lloyd said. The U.S. State Department and British Foreign Office advise those traveling near the Somali coast to use extreme caution because of the recent pirate attacks. Last week, the Australian government issued a similar warning about travel to the region. The advice also urged Australian ships "to apply a robust and layered protective security regime" when traveling through the area. -- CNN's Frederik Pleitgen contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**BERLIN, Germany (CNN) —** A German cruise line said Tuesday that it plans to fly passengers over the Gulf of Aden rather than sail them through the region because of fears of pirate attacks.

*U.S. Navy image of pirates operating off the coast of Somalia in October this year.*

Hapag-Lloyd Cruises said all 246 passengers and most of the crew aboard the *MS Columbus*, which is currently at the beginning of an around-the-world cruise, will disembark at an undisclosed port and fly to Dubai to continue their journey. The company described the move as a precautionary measure.

Pirate attacks in the waters off Somalia have surged this year, with pirates launching increasingly brazen assaults on ever-larger targets. According to the International Maritime Bureau, pirates have attacked nearly 100 vessels off Somalia’s coast so far this year and successfully hijacked almost 40.

Freight and cargo ships, cruise liners, and private yachts have all come under attack. In many hijackings, pirates hold crew members and passengers hostage while demanding a ransom.

The problem has forced companies such as Hapag-Lloyd, whose ships travel through the Gulf of Aden, to develop new plans, including strengthening security measures or changing routes. Last month, one shipping company announced that it would bypass the region altogether, sailing around the Cape of Good Hope instead and adding thousands of kilometers to its voyages.

Read more about how to solve the pirate problem here.

Hapag-Lloyd said that a general travel warning for the area issued by the German Foreign Ministry influenced its decision. However, the company also said it had requested naval protection from the German government and that the request was denied.

Representatives of Hapag-Lloyd and the German Defense Ministry could not immediately be reached for further comment.

The passengers aboard the *Columbus* began the first leg of their world cruise in Genoa, Italy, on November 28 and are scheduled to arrive in Dubai on December 17, according to Hapag-Lloyd’s website. Subsequent stops include Singapore; Bali, Indonesia; and Sydney, Australia.

Hapag-Lloyd said that after the passengers and most of the crew disembark, the *Columbus* will sail through the Gulf of Aden with a skeleton crew. Passengers will stay at a five-star hotel in Dubai for three days until the ship arrives to take them back on board, the company said.

Both the crew and passengers support the safety measure, according to Hapag-Lloyd.

The U.S. State Department and the British Foreign Office advise travelers near the Somali coast to exercise extreme caution because of the recent pirate attacks. Last week, the Australian government issued a similar warning regarding travel to the region. The advisory also urged Australian ships “to apply a robust and layered protective security regime” when traveling through the area.

— CNN’s Frederik Pleitgen contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
BERLIN, Germany (CNN) — Concern over piracy has prompted a German cruise operator to transport passengers by air across the Gulf of Aden rather than carry them through the area by ship, the company announced Tuesday.

A U.S. Navy photograph shows pirates active off Somalia’s coastline in October of this year.

Hapag-Lloyd Cruises said the MS Columbus, which is beginning a voyage around the world, will stop at a port whose location has not been disclosed. All 246 passengers and the majority of the crew will leave the vessel there and fly to Dubai, where the trip will resume. The company described the arrangement as a safety precaution.

Piracy near Somalia has increased sharply this year, with attackers pursuing larger vessels and carrying out more daring operations. International Maritime Bureau figures show that almost 100 ships have been attacked off the Somali coast so far this year, and nearly 40 of them were successfully seized.

The targets have included cargo and freight vessels, passenger cruise ships and privately owned yachts. During many such incidents, pirates hold crews and passengers captive while seeking ransom payments.

Shipping operators that travel through the Gulf of Aden, including Hapag-Lloyd, have consequently been forced to revise their plans by improving security or selecting alternative routes. Last month, one shipping company said it would avoid the region entirely and navigate around the Cape of Good Hope instead, adding thousands of kilometers to its journeys.

More information on possible solutions to the piracy problem is available here.

Hapag-Lloyd said its decision was influenced in part by a broad travel advisory for the region from Germany’s Foreign Ministry. It also said the German government had rejected the company’s request for protection from naval forces.

CNN was unable to immediately contact representatives of either Hapag-Lloyd or the German Defense Ministry for additional comment.

According to Hapag-Lloyd’s website, Columbus passengers departed Genoa, Italy, on November 28 for the opening stage of the global cruise and are scheduled to reach Dubai on December 17. Later destinations include Singapore; Bali, Indonesia; and Sydney, Australia.

Once the passengers and most crew members have gone ashore, the Columbus will cross the Gulf of Aden with only a minimal crew, Hapag-Lloyd said. Travelers will spend three days at a five-star Dubai hotel while waiting for the vessel to arrive, after which they will return aboard. The company said passengers and crew alike support the security measure.

Because of the recent surge in pirate activity, both the U.S. State Department and the British Foreign Office recommend that people traveling near Somalia’s coast exercise extreme caution. Australia issued a comparable warning last week. Its guidance also called on Australian vessels passing through the area “to apply a robust and layered protective security regime.”

CNN’s Frederik Pleitgen contributed to this report.
